source.title: Interpretable Debiasing of Vision-Language Models for Social Fairness
source.authors: Na-Min An; Yoonna Jang; Yusuke Hirota; Ryo Hachiuma; I. Augenstein; Hyunjung Shim

record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE-derived social neurons as a tool for debiasing VLMs. Its findings concern that method’s performance, not the neuron-pole audit shares or other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports debiasing and neuron-specificity results for its own SAE-based method. These do not test the listed versions’ claims about general neuron-job shares, scale, classic vision examples, attribution graphs, or explanation accuracy on held-out activations. It also cites other work on SAEs and neuron interpretability; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on VLM encoder outputs and uses selected SAE latents ('social neurons') as a debiasing tool. It reports its own method's bias and general-performance results. It does not audit the share of a model's own neurons with one job, nor examine InceptionV1 examples, attribution graphs, or simulation-based explanation scoring. SAE latents are a trained replacement basis, not the model's neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAE-identified social neurons can be deactivated to reduce social bias in VLMs and LVLMs with minimal loss of general performance. They also say the strength of the intervention (α) must be chosen carefully, since excessive modulation distorts semantic representations.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains SAEs on encoder activations, selects social-attribute neurons, and modulates them during inference; it does not reproduce the neuron-pole audit method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported intervention effects vary with the SAE decoded-feature weight α, the selected neuron group, modality, training/probing dataset, and model; the authors describe a trade-off between bias mitigation and general performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected SAE latents in CLIP encoders show attribute-aligned top-activating images. Ablating them reduces the targeted bias more than ablating random latents, with some cross-attribute spillover (age latents also reduce gender skew). The ablation study notes that latents from other training datasets mix attributes, e.g. female plus hairstyle.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents selected for social-attribute specificity in VLM encoders are largely, but not fully, single-attribute, and the purity depends on the SAE training data.

record.problems: The qualitative neuron-semantic evidence is based on visualizations; the paper does not test explanations on held-out activations. The reported neuron findings are limited to selected social-attribute SAE features and do not establish general one-job interpretations for ordinary model neurons.
record.rows_left_out: Most results in Tables 1–4 and the supplementary material report the performance of the paper’s own debiasing method or compare it with other debiasing methods; they do not test a listed claim version and were not extracted as rows.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and its 90/7/2–4% shares.
Shares across other LLMs, dense and MoE, and scale.
InceptionV1 cat/car neuron and recursive generalization.
Architecture, regularization and tools as causes; interpretable-share estimates.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Explanations from activating examples failing to predict firing.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's own motivation cites model neurons as often polysemantic (a cited claim, not tested). Its 'neurons' are SAE latents, so nothing here measures how often raw model neurons are monosemantic.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and the stated proportions of one-job, two-job, and not-yet-understood neuron poles.
Interpretability shares across other models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or trillion-parameter scale.
InceptionV1’s cat-and-car neuron and the proposed pose/recursive-generalization interpretation.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain messy neurons or change the share of interpretable neurons, including the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Attribution graphs, whether model neurons suffice to explain behaviour, and comparison with replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations written from activating examples fail to predict activations on other examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-B/16)
rows.operation_detail: Visualized top-activating images for SAE-selected social neurons

conditions.value: gender, age, and race social neurons

rows.measure: Semantic alignment of top-activating images with the social attribute assigned to each neuron
rows.value: The authors describe the selected social neurons as having high semantic purity; their top-activating images correspond to a single social attribute.
rows.note: This is qualitative evidence about SAE-selected social neurons, not a measurement of the share of all neurons with one main job.
rows.check: Qualitative top-activating images for hand-picked SAE latents selected for attribute specificity. These are selection outputs, not a share of model neurons. 'Observed' is not meaningful for any version.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-B/16)
rows.note: The paper describes this as an intersectional effect and attributes it to age-gender correlation in the data; this result does not test any listed version.
rows.check: A performance result of the paper's own debiasing method (age-latent ablation lowering gender Max Skew 10.6 to 9.2 versus random). It bears on no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
